problem.title: Card-fraud scoring service
problem.context: A payments company needs in-environment real-time fraud scoring at up to 15,000 transactions per second, with delayed labels, historical auditability and a seven-person delivery team.

requirements.text: Score every card transaction before the authorization decision, using the cardholder's recent activity (for example, the spending of the last hour and the last day).
Update the model as new confirmed fraud cases arrive.
For any past score, show which model version and which input values produced it.
During a seasonal peak of 15,000 transactions per second, a score comes back within 30 ms at the 99th percentile.
When the scoring service or one of its data sources fails, authorizations go on. The business accepts weaker fraud detection for up to 15 minutes, but no authorization may fail because of scoring.
An auditor asks about a score from up to 13 months ago. Within one working day the team answers with the model version, the input values and the training data that model was built from.
When the fraud loss rate rises in one segment, a retrained model can be in production within 48 hours, after it has been compared with the current model on recent transactions.
Card data must stay inside the company's PCI-certified environment: no external service may process it.
Seven people build and run the system, with no dedicated ML platform team.

points.description: 1. The system trains models in batches, versions data in a code repository, and serves predictions through a local real-time API using features stored in general-purpose data stores. A CI/CD pipeline deploys updates, prediction-service performance is tested, production usage and behavior are tracked, and a previous model can be redeployed and switched back when needed. 2. Trade-off: This provides straightforward automation, rollback, and operational visibility without adopting MLOps. It gives up specialized MLOps capabilities and may leave feature management, training orchestration, and model lifecycle coordination less integrated.

The system uses an MLOps orchestrator to incrementally train models from versioned data and feature-store features, then deploys multiple model versions through a real-time microservice. It logs inputs and predictions for monitoring and uses A/B testing to compare versions and guide promotion. Trade-off: This gains reproducible data management, continuous adaptation, controlled experimentation, and observable serving. It gives up simplicity: orchestrating incremental training, maintaining several production versions, and monitoring their behavior require substantial infrastructure and operational effort, while incremental updates can increase drift risk.

The system uses a feature store to support hybrid online/offline serving and hybrid batch/incremental training. An MLOps CI/CD pipeline versions data, tests hypotheses, deploys multiple model versions, and tracks their production usage, inputs, outputs, interpretability, and fairness. Trade-off: This gains flexible low-latency serving, continuous adaptation, reproducibility, controlled releases, and richer production oversight. It gives up simplicity: coordinating feature consistency, incremental and batch training, versioned data, multiple deployments, and comprehensive monitoring increases infrastructure and operational complexity.

A batch-trained model is built, evaluated, and validated in an automated pipeline, with data kept in a technology-specific version repository. A local real-time service exposes predictions; CI/CD deploys it, prediction-service performance is tested, production activity and outputs are tracked, and rollback can restore an earlier model version. Trade-off: This provides reproducibility, automated delivery, operational visibility, and recovery while retaining simple feature storage. Trade-off: Batch learning may make predictions less current, while avoiding MLOps limits specialized lifecycle automation and generic feature stores may weaken consistency and access support.

A feature store supplies consistent features to a batch-based training process and a real-time model-serving microservice. An automated model-building pipeline evaluates and validates models, an ML orchestrator coordinates workflows, data versioning supports reproducibility, and multiple validated model versions can run in production while predictions and system data are monitored; evidence-based hypothesis testing guides pipeline tests. Trade-off: This improves repeatability, deployment flexibility, and observability, but adds operational complexity, storage and orchestration overhead, and risks inconsistent behavior or maintenance burden across simultaneously deployed model versions.

A feature store and versioned data repository feed batch training, with evidence-based tests and CI/CD automating model releases. Multiple model versions are deployed through hybrid online/offline serving, while production tracking monitors usage, inputs, outputs, interpretability, and fairness. Trade-off: This gains reproducibility, controlled experimentation, and broad operational visibility, but batch learning may reduce responsiveness to new data and maintaining multiple versions increases serving and monitoring complexity. The “No MLOps” choice conflicts with the CI/CD, versioning, testing, and tracking practices, which are characteristic MLOps capabilities.

Batch training uses versioned data from a feature store, while CI/CD tests prediction-service performance and deploys models to a local real-time serving API. Production usage, inputs, outputs, interpretability, and fairness are tracked, with rollback available to a previous model version. Trade-off: This provides reproducibility, operational visibility, and recovery while keeping serving responsive. It gives up broader MLOps lifecycle coordination and may leave batch-trained models less current between releases.

This system trains models in batches through an automated build pipeline, tests trained-model quality, versions training data in a dedicated repository, and delivers deployments through CI/CD. A local prediction API serves real-time scores from features in general-purpose data stores; production usage, inputs, outputs, interpretability, and fairness are tracked, with rollback available to restore the prior model. Trade-off: It gains repeatability, traceability, visibility, and recovery, but gives up specialized feature-store capabilities and integrated MLOps support, increasing coordination and operational burden.

A feature store supplies consistent training and serving features, while versioned data feeds an orchestrated model-building pipeline that batch-trains, evaluates, and validates models. The resulting models are deployed as multiple concurrent microservice versions, enabling A/B testing, with MLOps tracking usage, inputs, outputs, interpretability, and fairness in production. Trade-off: This provides reproducibility, automation, controlled comparisons, and rich oversight, but requires substantial orchestration, feature-store, version-management, and monitoring infrastructure, plus added operational complexity and storage for concurrent models and tracked data.

A feature store and versioned data repository support batch training, while CI/CD tests trained-model quality and deploys multiple model versions. Predictions are served through a hybrid online/offline architecture, with production usage, inputs, outputs, interpretability, and fairness tracked. Trade-off: This gains reproducibility, deployment flexibility, and operational visibility, but batch learning may reduce responsiveness to new data and maintaining multiple versions increases complexity. The “No MLOps” choice conflicts with the selected CI/CD, tracking, versioning, and feature-store practices, which are characteristic MLOps capabilities.

A batch-trained model uses versioned data and a feature store, is tested for quality, and served through a local real-time API. A CI/CD pipeline deploys it, with production tracking and rollback to the previous model version when needed. Trade-off: This gains reproducibility, operational recovery, and visibility into model behavior, but gives up MLOps-specific coordination and automation despite using CI/CD, potentially leaving model lifecycle practices less comprehensive. The “No MLOps” choice conflicts somewhat with CI/CD for ML because it rejects the broader discipline that the pipeline supports.

1. A batch-trained model uses a feature store and versioned data repository, then is deployed as a real-time prediction microservice through a CI/CD pipeline. Production usage, inputs, outputs, interpretability, fairness, and service performance are tracked, while a previous model version can be redeployed and activated if needed. 2. Trade-off: This provides reproducible data, automated delivery, operational visibility, and rapid rollback. It gives up continuously updated learning and the broader coordination, automation, and governance typically associated with MLOps, while batch retraining may leave the model less responsive to changing data.

approaches.idea: What if local real-time serving, batch retraining and rollback keep operations focused while versioning and tracking support audits?
What if an orchestrated microservice and concurrent models maximize experimentation and automation?
What if hybrid serving, a feature store and multiple versions balance online scoring with offline lifecycle work?
What if a feature store and explicit tracking pair with batch updates and rollback, without MLOps?
